aloe_vera.conservation_status: Not threatened (widely cultivated; wild origin uncertain)
aloe_vera.brief: A succulent plant with thick, fleshy leaves that store a clear gel. It is grown worldwide for skin care and traditional medicine.
aloe_vera.habitat: Dry, warm regions; grown in gardens, pots and farms.
aloe_vera.uses: Gel is used for burns, skin care and cosmetics; juice is used in traditional medicine.
aloe_vera.threats: Few threats, since it is widely cultivated.
fun_facts: It stores water in its leaves, so it survives long dry spells.
It belongs to the family Asphodelaceae.

asian_elephant.brief: The largest land mammal in Asia, living in family herds led by an older female. Smaller than the African elephant, with smaller ears.
asian_elephant.habitat: Forests and grasslands of India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
asian_elephant.diet: Herbivore: grasses, bark, roots and fruit.
asian_elephant.threats: Habitat fragmentation, human-elephant conflict and poaching for ivory.
fun_facts: The trunk has tens of thousands of muscles.
Elephants communicate using low-frequency sounds.

banyan.brief: A large fig tree that grows aerial roots which become new trunks. It is India's national tree.
banyan.habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions of the Indian subcontinent; planted in villages and temples.
banyan.uses: Shade tree; bark and latex are used in traditional medicine; sacred in Indian culture.
banyan.threats: Mostly safe, but old trees can be lost to urban expansion.
fun_facts: One tree can spread over a huge area through its prop roots.
The Great Banyan in Kolkata is among the widest trees in the world.

bengal_monitor.conservation_status: Least Concern (IUCN); protected under Indian law
bengal_monitor.brief: A large lizard found across South Asia, often seen on the ground or climbing trees. It has a long forked tongue like a snake.
bengal_monitor.habitat: Forests, scrubland, farmland and the edges of villages.
bengal_monitor.diet: Carnivore: insects, rodents, eggs, small reptiles and carrion.
bengal_monitor.threats: Hunted for meat and skin; killed out of fear; habitat loss.
fun_facts: It is protected under India's Wildlife Protection Act.
It flicks its tongue to smell its surroundings.

brahmi.conservation_status: Not globally threatened; over-harvesting is a concern
brahmi.brief: A small creeping herb of wet places that is well known in Ayurveda as a memory and brain tonic.
brahmi.habitat: Marshes, wetlands and the banks of ponds and streams.
brahmi.uses: Used in Ayurvedic medicine, mainly for memory and calming effects.
brahmi.threats: Over-collection from the wild for medicine and loss of wetlands.
fun_facts: Its Sanskrit name is linked to 'Brahma', the creator.
It grows well in waterlogged soil.

chital.brief: A graceful deer with a reddish-brown coat covered in white spots all year. It lives in herds and is a main prey of the tiger and leopard.
chital.habitat: Open forests and grasslands of India, Sri Lanka and Nepal.
chital.diet: Herbivore: grasses, leaves, flowers and fruit.
chital.threats: Poaching and habitat loss, but numbers are stable overall.
fun_facts: Males grow branched antlers and shed them every year.
Chital often follow langurs to eat the fruit they drop.

common_kingfisher.brief: A small, brightly coloured bird with a blue back and orange underparts that dives into water to catch fish.
common_kingfisher.habitat: Rivers, ponds, lakes and streams across Europe and Asia.
common_kingfisher.diet: Carnivore: small fish, water insects and tadpoles.
common_kingfisher.threats: Water pollution and loss of river banks for nesting.
fun_facts: It nests in tunnels dug into river banks.
It can dive from a perch and catch fish in a split second.

daisy.brief: A small flower with white petals around a yellow centre, common on lawns and meadows.
daisy.habitat: Lawns, meadows and grassy roadsides in temperate regions.
daisy.uses: Mostly ornamental; leaves and flowers are edible and used in traditional medicine.
daisy.threats: Not threatened; often treated as a lawn weed.
fun_facts: The flower head closes at night and opens in the morning.
The name 'daisy' comes from 'day's eye'.

dandelion.brief: A yellow flower that turns into a white puffball of seeds carried by the wind. It grows almost anywhere.
dandelion.habitat: Fields, lawns, roadsides and waste ground worldwide.
dandelion.uses: Leaves are eaten as greens; root is used in herbal teas and medicine.
dandelion.threats: Not threatened; regarded as a weed.
fun_facts: Each seed has a tiny parachute that helps it fly far.
The whole plant is edible.

giant_milkweed.brief: A large shrub with waxy purple-white flowers and a milky, toxic sap. It is common on dry wasteland in India.
giant_milkweed.habitat: Dry wasteland, roadsides and scrubland of South and Southeast Asia.
giant_milkweed.uses: Used in traditional medicine and religious offerings; fibres from the stem have been used. The sap is poisonous.
giant_milkweed.threats: Not threatened; grows easily in poor soil.
fun_facts: It is a host plant for butterflies such as the Plain Tiger.
Its flowers are offered in some Hindu worship.

gotu_kola.brief: A small creeping herb with round, fan-shaped leaves. It is used in traditional Indian and Chinese medicine.
gotu_kola.habitat: Damp ground, ditches and swamps in tropical and subtropical regions.
gotu_kola.uses: Used for skin healing and as a herbal tonic; leaves are eaten as a salad green in parts of Asia.
gotu_kola.threats: Over-collection and loss of wetland habitat locally.
fun_facts: It spreads by runners along the ground.
It is also called Mandukaparni in Ayurveda.

hibiscus.brief: A shrub with large, showy flowers, usually red. It is a very common garden plant in India.
hibiscus.habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions; grown in gardens and as hedges.
hibiscus.uses: Ornamental; flowers are used in worship, hair care and herbal drinks.
hibiscus.threats: Not threatened because it is widely grown.
fun_facts: Hibiscus flowers last only a day or two.
It is the national flower of Malaysia.

indian_cobra.conservation_status: Least Concern (IUCN); protected under Indian law
indian_cobra.brief: A venomous snake that spreads its hood when threatened. It is one of India's 'Big Four' venomous snakes.
indian_cobra.habitat: Forests, farmland, villages and rocky areas across the Indian subcontinent.
indian_cobra.diet: Carnivore: rats, frogs, lizards and other snakes.
indian_cobra.threats: Killed out of fear, road deaths and habitat loss.
fun_facts: It plays an important role in controlling rats.
Its bite needs urgent medical treatment with antivenom.

indian_crested_porcupine.brief: A large rodent covered in sharp black and white quills. It is active mostly at night.
indian_crested_porcupine.habitat: Forests, grasslands, hills and farmland across South Asia.
indian_crested_porcupine.diet: Herbivore: roots, tubers, fruit and crops.
indian_crested_porcupine.threats: Hunting for meat and killing as a crop pest.
fun_facts: It rattles its quills to warn predators.
It lives in burrows and caves.

indian_peafowl.brief: The male, the peacock, has a long, colourful train of feathers that it fans out to attract females. It is India's national bird.
indian_peafowl.habitat: Forests, farmland and villages across the Indian subcontinent.
indian_peafowl.diet: Omnivore: seeds, insects, small reptiles and fruit.
indian_peafowl.threats: Poisoning from pesticides and hunting in some areas.
fun_facts: The train is not the tail but long upper tail covert feathers.
Peacocks dance with their feathers open, especially in the monsoon.

indian_rhinoceros.brief: Also called the greater one-horned rhino, it has a single black horn and thick skin folded into plate-like sections.
indian_rhinoceros.habitat: Tall grasslands and floodplains of Assam and Nepal. Kaziranga National Park holds most of the population.
indian_rhinoceros.diet: Herbivore: grasses, leaves, fruit and aquatic plants.
indian_rhinoceros.threats: Poaching for horn, floods and loss of grassland.
fun_facts: It is a good swimmer.
Conservation efforts have brought it back from near extinction.

indian_rock_python.brief: One of the largest snakes in India. It is non-venomous and kills prey by squeezing it.
indian_rock_python.habitat: Forests, grasslands, marshes and rocky hills of South Asia.
indian_rock_python.diet: Carnivore: deer, birds, rodents and other small animals.
indian_rock_python.threats: Hunting for skin and meat, and habitat loss.
fun_facts: It can go weeks without eating after a large meal.
The female coils around her eggs to keep them warm.

mango.brief: A tropical fruit tree whose sweet fruit is eaten around the world. The mango is India's national fruit.
mango.habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions; grown in orchards and home gardens.
mango.uses: Fruit is eaten fresh or in juice, pickles and sweets; leaves and wood have traditional uses.
mango.threats: Wild forms are rare due to forest loss; cultivated trees are common.
fun_facts: India is one of the world's largest mango producers.
There are hundreds of varieties, such as Alphonso and Dasheri.

monarch_butterfly.brief: An orange and black butterfly famous for its long migration. Its bright colours warn predators that it tastes bad.
monarch_butterfly.habitat: Open meadows, fields and gardens, mainly in North America.
monarch_butterfly.diet: Caterpillars eat milkweed; adults drink nectar from flowers.
monarch_butterfly.threats: Loss of milkweed, pesticides, climate change and loss of overwintering forests.
fun_facts: Migration takes several generations to complete.
Milkweed makes it toxic to predators.

moringa.brief: A fast-growing tree with long drumstick-shaped pods. Its leaves and pods are very nutritious.
moringa.habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions; grown in farms and home gardens.
moringa.uses: Pods (drumsticks) are used in sambar and curries; leaves are eaten as greens or powder; seeds can help clean water.
moringa.threats: Not threatened because it is widely grown.
fun_facts: It grows well in dry, poor soils.
It is nicknamed the 'miracle tree'.

neem.brief: A large evergreen tree known for its bitter leaves. Every part of it is used in medicine, farming and daily life in India.
neem.habitat: Dry tropical regions of the Indian subcontinent; planted along roads and in villages.
neem.uses: Twigs for brushing teeth, leaves and oil for skin care, and neem extracts as natural pesticides.
fun_facts: Neem twigs have been used as natural toothbrushes for centuries.
Neem oil is used in organic farming.

nilgiri_tahr.brief: A sturdy mountain goat found only in the Western Ghats of southern India. It is the state animal of Tamil Nadu.
nilgiri_tahr.habitat: Steep grassy slopes and rocky cliffs of the Nilgiri and Anamalai hills in the Western Ghats.
nilgiri_tahr.threats: Habitat loss, hunting and limited range.
fun_facts: It climbs steep cliffs with ease.
Only a few thousand remain in the wild.

peepal.brief: A large fig tree with heart-shaped leaves that is sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism. Buddha is said to have gained enlightenment under one.
peepal.habitat: Tropical Asia; planted near temples, villages and roadsides.
peepal.uses: Shade tree; leaves, bark and fruit are used in traditional medicine; sacred in several religions.
fun_facts: Its leaves have a long tip that helps rain water drip off quickly.
The Bodhi Tree in Bodh Gaya is a peepal.

rhesus_macaque.brief: A brown-grey monkey that lives in large groups. It is commonly seen near temples and towns in India.
rhesus_macaque.habitat: Forests, farmland, temples and cities across South and Southeast Asia.
rhesus_macaque.diet: Omnivore: fruit, seeds, leaves, insects and food from people.
rhesus_macaque.threats: Not threatened, but conflict with humans is common.
fun_facts: It lives in social groups with clear rank.
It has been widely used in medical research.

sacred_lotus.brief: An aquatic plant with large round leaves and pink or white flowers that rise above the water. It is India's national flower.
sacred_lotus.habitat: Shallow ponds, lakes and slow-moving water across Asia.
sacred_lotus.uses: Seeds, roots and stems are eaten; petals and leaves are used in worship and traditional medicine.
sacred_lotus.threats: Pollution and drainage of wetlands can affect wild populations locally.
fun_facts: Lotus leaves repel water and dirt (the 'lotus effect').
Seeds can stay viable for hundreds of years.

sunflower.brief: A tall plant with a large yellow flower head that follows the sun when young. It is grown for its seeds and oil.
sunflower.habitat: Open, sunny fields; native to North America and grown worldwide.
sunflower.uses: Seeds are eaten as snacks; sunflower oil is used for cooking.
sunflower.threats: Not threatened because it is widely cultivated.
fun_facts: Young flowers turn to face the sun during the day.
The flower head is made of hundreds of tiny flowers.

tiger.brief: The largest living cat, with an orange coat and dark stripes. Each tiger's stripe pattern is unique. It is India's national animal.
tiger.habitat: Forests, mangroves (such as the Sundarbans) and grasslands across South and Southeast Asia.
tiger.diet: Carnivore: deer, wild boar and gaur.
tiger.threats: Habitat loss, poaching and conflict with humans.
fun_facts: Tigers are strong swimmers.
Project Tiger (1973) helped protect the species in India.
